articles.title: The Donkey Who Saw the Sword
articles.dek: A prophet for hire beat the animal that was saving his life. Peter remembered that strange afternoon and found in it a warning, and a mercy, for anyone whose eyes have been clouded by wanting more.
articles.quote: Before you strike whatever is blocking your road, ask what it might be seeing that you cannot.
articles.body:
On the morning of April 12, 1955, church bells began ringing in towns across America. In Ann Arbor, Michigan, a scientist named Thomas Francis Jr. had just told a packed room of reporters that the polio vaccine developed by a young researcher named Jonas Salk was safe and effective. Parents cried at their kitchen tables, and shopkeepers taped hand-lettered signs to their windows that read, "Thank you, Dr. Salk." Only three years earlier the United States had recorded nearly 58,000 polio cases, and summer had become the season mothers feared most, with public pools shut and children kept indoors against a disease that could leave them in leg braces or inside an iron lung.

That evening the broadcaster Edward R. Murrow asked Salk who owned the patent on the vaccine. Salk seemed almost puzzled by the question. "Well, the people, I would say," he answered. "There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?" Historians note that the vaccine might have been difficult to patent in any case, but the spirit of his answer is what the world kept. Salk lived the rest of his life on a researcher's salary, and the gift travelled to children everywhere, including the Philippines, where vaccination drives would one day reach barangays very far from any laboratory.

Keep that picture in mind, a man holding something priceless who chose to give it away, because Peter's second letter sets beside it a man who did the opposite. Peter wrote this letter near the end of his life, knowing, as he put it, that "I will soon put it aside" (2 Peter 1:14), meaning the tent of his body. With the time he had left, he wanted the churches to hold fast to the true word of God, "a light shining in a dark place" (2 Peter 1:19), because "prophets, though human, spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:21). Then he turned to a darker subject: "there will be false teachers among you" (2 Peter 2:1). To show what such teachers look like, he reached back into Israel's history for one of the strangest stories in the whole Bible.

The story is told in Numbers 22. Israel had camped on the plains of Moab, and Balak, the frightened king of Moab, sent messengers with fees in their hands to a famous seer named Balaam. The king's request was simple: come and curse these people for me. God told Balaam plainly that Israel was blessed and must not be cursed. Yet when a second, larger delegation arrived with promises of great honor, Balaam invited them to stay the night while he asked God again, as though the answer might change if the price went up. God let him go, with a firm warning to speak only what he was given, and early the next morning Balaam saddled his donkey and rode off toward the king's silver.

On the road stood the angel of the LORD with a drawn sword in his hand. Balaam saw nothing, but his donkey saw everything. She swerved off the road into a field, and Balaam beat her back onto the path. Further on, the road narrowed between two vineyard walls, and when the angel appeared again she pressed herself against the stone and crushed her rider's foot, so he beat her again. At last the angel stood in a place so narrow there was no room to turn, and the donkey simply lay down under him. Balaam, furious, struck her with his staff.

Then something happened that no one in Moab could have imagined. "The LORD opened the donkey's mouth, and it said to Balaam, 'What have I done to you to make you beat me these three times?'" (Numbers 22:28). Balaam, apparently too angry to be astonished, argued back: "You have made a fool of me! If only I had a sword in my hand, I would kill you right now" (Numbers 22:29). There is a dark comedy in that line, since a sword was at that very moment pointed at his own chest. Only when the LORD opened Balaam's eyes did he see the angel, who told him that if the donkey had not turned aside, he would have killed Balaam and spared her (Numbers 22:33). The animal he had beaten three times had saved his life three times.

Centuries later, Peter summed up that whole afternoon in two sentences:

"They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Bezer, who loved the wages of wickedness. But he was rebuked for his wrongdoing by a donkey, an animal without speech, who spoke with a human voice and restrained the prophet's madness." (2 Peter 2:15–16)

The word Peter chose for "madness" is the Greek paraphronia, which appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It literally means being beside one's mind, thinking alongside the truth without ever touching it. Peter could have called Balaam wicked or disobedient, and both would have been true. Instead he described a man whose love of money had quietly pushed him out of his right mind. The famous seer, the man people paid precisely because he could see what others could not, was the only one on that road who was blind. A simple donkey, wanting nothing from the king of Moab, saw the danger at once.

One way to read this is that greed works less like a crime and more like a fog. Peter says the false teachers of his day would "exploit you with fabricated stories" (2 Peter 2:3), and the verb he uses there, emporeuomai, is the root of our word "emporium." They would turn people into merchandise. Later in the chapter he gives the principle underneath it: "people are slaves to whatever has mastered them" (2 Peter 2:19). Balaam never stopped speaking about God, and in the chapters that follow he even pronounced beautiful blessings over Israel. Yet Scripture remembers that he later advised Moab on how to lead Israel into sin (Numbers 31:16), and both Jude 11 and Revelation 2:14 name him as a warning. A person can keep saying the right words while the heart slowly rides toward the silver.

The mercy in the story is easy to miss. God placed something stubborn in Balaam's path because he did not want Balaam to die on that road. The donkey's refusal was a rescue, and so were the crushed foot and the animal lying flat in the dust. This suggests a gentle question for anyone who feels blocked right now. Perhaps a promotion keeps slipping away, or a deal you were sure of has collapsed, or a friend keeps saying, uncomfortably, that something about your plan worries them. Before you strike whatever is blocking your road, ask what it might be seeing that you cannot.

Most of us will never be offered a king's fortune to curse a nation, but the smaller roads are very familiar. We meet them in the extra commission that requires bending the truth a little, the side income that slowly eats our Sundays and our children's evenings, and the online preacher who promises that faith is mainly a path to wealth. Peter's answer to all of them is the one he gave at the start of this passage: keep your eyes on the word God has already spoken, the lamp in the dark place, "until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts" (2 Peter 1:19). That light is what clears the fog.

Jonas Salk's question still has a way of cutting through it, too. Could you patent the sun? The things God has placed in your hands, whether a skill, a salary, a home, or simply time, were never meant to be held so tightly that they cloud your sight. Today, give one of them away freely, with no wage expected, perhaps by teaching someone what you know or by paying for a neighbor's need without telling anyone. Open hands have a way of keeping eyes open. And if something stubborn is lying down in your road this week, thank God for it before you raise your staff, because the One who sent a donkey to stop a prophet still loves his people too much to let them ride past the sword.

articles.title: The Gate God Closed Behind Him
articles.dek: In Ezekiel's vision, the glory of God comes home through the east gate, and then that gate is shut for good. It may be the most tender locked door in the Bible.
articles.quote: God shut the gate behind him so that you would never again have to wonder whether he is about to leave.
articles.body:
In May 1873, a thirty-three-year-old Belgian priest named Damien de Veuster stepped off a boat onto the Kalaupapa peninsula on the Hawaiian island of Molokai. Behind the settlement rose some of the tallest sea cliffs in the world, and in front of it lay a rough and often unforgiving sea. Since 1866 the Hawaiian government had been sending people with leprosy (today called Hansen's disease) to that isolated strip of land, and many arrived believing they had been sent there to die. Visitors came and went, and officials inspected the place and sailed away again. The church's plan was for priests to take turns serving the colony for a few weeks at a time, so that no one would have to remain too long.

Damien asked to stay. He dressed wounds and built homes with his own hands, and he learned the names of people the rest of the world preferred to forget. For years he opened his sermons with "my brethren," and after he contracted the disease himself, he is remembered as beginning one sermon with the words "We lepers." He died at Kalawao in April 1889, and in 2009 the Catholic Church canonized him as Saint Damien of Molokai. What the people of that peninsula remembered most about him was wonderfully simple: he was the one who never got back on the boat.

Something of that same ache, and that same answer, sits at the heart of today's reading from Ezekiel. To feel its weight, it helps to know what happened before it.

Ezekiel was a priest who never had the chance to serve in the temple. He was carried off to Babylon in 597 BC with the first wave of exiles, and there, beside the Kebar River, God called him to be a prophet. In one of his earliest visions (Ezekiel 8 to 11), he watched something no Israelite had ever imagined, as the glory of the LORD left Jerusalem's temple in slow, heartbreaking stages. It rose from the inner sanctuary "and moved to the threshold of the temple" (Ezekiel 10:4), then paused "at the entrance of the east gate of the LORD's house" (Ezekiel 10:19), and finally "went up from within the city and stopped above the mountain east of it" (Ezekiel 11:23). It was like watching someone you love linger at the doorway, stand for a moment at the gate, and then walk up the hill and out of sight. A few years later, in 586 BC, Babylon burned the temple to the ground.

Now move ahead to Ezekiel 40, which is dated "in the twenty-fifth year of our exile... in the fourteenth year after the fall of the city" (Ezekiel 40:1). By then the ruins had sat cold for fourteen years, and children who were small when Jerusalem fell had grown into adults who had never seen the temple. God gives Ezekiel a long vision of a new sanctuary, measured gate by gate and wall by wall, and in chapter 43 the moment the whole book has been aching for finally arrives. Ezekiel is brought to the gate facing east, the very direction in which the glory had disappeared, "and I saw the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east. His voice was like the roar of rushing waters, and the land was radiant with his glory" (Ezekiel 43:2). The prophet falls on his face. "The glory of the LORD entered the temple through the gate facing east" (Ezekiel 43:4), and the Spirit lifts Ezekiel into the inner court, where he sees that "the glory of the LORD filled the temple" (Ezekiel 43:5). God comes home by the same road he used to leave, and then he speaks: "This is where I will live among the Israelites forever" (Ezekiel 43:7).

The word translated "live" comes from the Hebrew shakan, which means to settle down and dwell. It shares a root with mishkan, the tabernacle, the tent where God camped among Israel in the wilderness. The word for "glory," kavod, carries the basic sense of weight or heaviness, so the glory of God is his weighty, substantial presence, the sheer realness of him. What returns to the temple in Ezekiel's vision is God himself, coming back to settle in among his people. He even names what had driven him away, saying, "Now let them put away from me their prostitution and the lifeless idols of their kings, and I will live among them forever" (Ezekiel 43:9).

Then comes a detail that most readers pass over quickly. A chapter later, Ezekiel is led back to that same eastern gate, "and it was shut" (Ezekiel 44:1).

The LORD said to me, "This gate is to remain shut. It must not be opened; no one may enter through it. It is to remain shut because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered through it." (Ezekiel 44:2)

At first glance a locked gate sounds cold, even unwelcoming. Part of its meaning is plainly reverence, since a doorway the King himself has used is set apart for him alone. Yet one way to read it, especially through the eyes of exiles who had watched God go, is as one of the most tender details in the entire prophecy. The east gate was the door of departure, and once God has come home through it, the door is sealed. This suggests that there will be no second leaving by that road, and that the gate he once walked out of in sorrow is now closed behind him in commitment.

Even the closed gate becomes a place of fellowship. "The prince himself is the only one who may sit inside the gateway to eat in the presence of the LORD" (Ezekiel 44:3). In the very spot where the goodbye once happened, a table is set, and a meal is eaten in God's presence. The prophecy closes with the new name of the city: "THE LORD IS THERE" (Ezekiel 48:35).

The rest of Scripture carries this promise forward. John writes that "the Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us" (John 1:14), using the Greek verb skēnoō, to pitch a tent, a clear echo of the tabernacle where God first camped with his people. The letter to the Hebrews holds on to God's own word: "Never will I leave you; never will I forsake you" (Hebrews 13:5). The God who once walked out of the east gate because of his people's sin came back, and in Jesus he came all the way down to stay with us.

Many Filipinos know the doorway goodbye well. Children of OFWs remember the parent who held them tightly at NAIA and then was gone for two years, with a balikbayan box arriving where a person used to be. Others carry a quieter story, of a father who left and never returned, or a friend who drifted away once life became hard. Those goodbyes teach the heart to brace itself, and we often carry that bracing into our faith, wondering whether God will eventually tire of us and head for the gate. Ezekiel 44:2 answers that fear directly. He came back to people who had given him every reason to stay away, and God shut the gate behind him so that you would never again have to wonder whether he is about to leave.

This passage also shapes the way we love one another. The people of Kalaupapa were healed by Damien's presence long before medicine could help them, because staying is one of the rarest gifts one person can give another. Somewhere in your life there is likely someone quietly watching to see whether you will remain: an aging parent, a friend in a long season of struggle, a spouse who is tired and afraid. Their situation may be beyond your power to fix, and staying is still well within your reach. You can close your own east gate by deciding in your heart that walking away is no longer an option you keep open, and then you can show it today with a phone call, a planned visit, or an unhurried meal at the same table.

Before you begin your work today, picture that shut gate on the east side of the temple, and thank God for coming back to you and settling in to stay. Then carry his faithfulness into one relationship where someone has grown used to people leaving. When you stay, in small and ordinary ways, you give them a living picture of the God whose name is written over every place he chooses to dwell: the LORD is there.

articles.title: The Work That Happens While You Sleep
articles.dek: Scientists have learned that the brain does its deepest cleaning only after we close our eyes. A song written by Israel's greatest builder seems to have known that God does some of his best work in the dark.
articles.quote: The God who builds the house also keeps the night watch, and he gives to his beloved even while they sleep.
articles.body:
In 2013, a team at the University of Rochester led by the Danish neuroscientist Maiken Nedergaard published a discovery about something every one of us does each night. They had been studying the brains of sleeping mice, and they found that during sleep the spaces between brain cells widened by roughly sixty percent. Through those widened channels flowed cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid that cushions the brain, rinsing through the tissue and carrying away the waste that piles up during a day of thinking, including proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease. The researchers named it the glymphatic system, and they observed that when the mice were awake, this cleansing slowed to a fraction of its nighttime pace.

Put simply, some of the most important care your brain will ever receive happens at an hour when you can contribute nothing to it. You cannot hurry it by trying harder, and you cannot do it while you are still bent over your desk at midnight. It begins only after you lie down and let the day go. The human body, it turns out, was designed from the beginning to receive a gift in the dark.

Three thousand years before anyone had a microscope, a Hebrew poet wrote a song about this very thing. Psalm 127 is one of fifteen "Songs of Ascents" (Psalms 120 to 134), short hymns that pilgrims most likely sang as they climbed the hill roads to Jerusalem for the great festivals. Its heading attributes it to Solomon, which makes it remarkable. Solomon was the master builder of Israel's history. He spent seven years building the temple (1 Kings 6:38) and thirteen more building his own palace (1 Kings 7:1). If anyone had reason to believe that great houses rise through great effort, it was the king who had supervised tens of thousands of laborers, stonecutters, and craftsmen.

Yet the song he leaves behind is about the limits of effort. It opens with a builder on the scaffolding, laying stone on stone. Then it pans to a watchman on the city wall, peering into the darkness for raiders who may or may not come. Finally it settles on an ordinary worker, up before the roosters and still at it long after the lamps are lit, eating what the Hebrew calls "the bread of anxious toil." These are the people every pilgrim knew, and many of them were the pilgrims themselves.

"Unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the guards stand watch in vain. In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for food to eat, for he grants sleep to those he loves." (Psalm 127:1–2)

The word translated "in vain" is the Hebrew shav', which means empty or hollow, like a jar that looks full until you lift it. Solomon uses it over and over in two short verses, as if pressing on a bruise. He is careful about what he says. The builders still build and the guards still stand watch; the psalm expects the work to go on. What it empties out is the belief that the whole outcome rests on our shoulders, that if we stop for even one night, everything we have made will fall.

The word "house" carries extra weight here. The Hebrew bayit can mean a building, a household, a family line, or the temple itself. Solomon grew up hearing the story of how his father David once wanted to build God a house, and how God answered through the prophet Nathan with a reversal: "The LORD declares to you that the LORD himself will establish a house for you" (2 Samuel 7:11). Before Solomon laid a single stone, his whole life already sat inside a house that God had promised to build.

The most tender detail in the psalm hides in the last phrase. The Hebrew word for "those he loves" is yedid, meaning beloved. When Solomon was born, God sent word through Nathan that the baby should also be called Jedidiah, "loved by the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:25). One way to read verse 2, then, is as a king quietly signing his own name. The man who built the most famous house in Israel says, in effect, that God gives rest to his yedid, and he knew he was one of them.

Many scholars also point out that the Hebrew of that line can be read another way: "he gives to his beloved in sleep," meaning that God provides for his people even while they lie unconscious. Solomon knew this from experience. The defining gift of his life, the wisdom he became famous for, came to him at Gibeon, where "the LORD appeared to Solomon during the night in a dream" (1 Kings 3:5). He went to bed a young, uncertain king and woke up carrying what he had asked for. His greatest equipment for the work arrived while he was doing nothing at all.

Jesus told a parable with the same heartbeat. "A man scatters seed on the ground. Night and day, whether he sleeps or gets up, the seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how" (Mark 4:26–27). The farmer plants, and then he goes to bed, and the growing happens on God's time. Even the psalm's second half, which turns to children as "a heritage from the LORD" (Psalm 127:3), points the same direction. A child is the clearest example in human life of something precious that we receive and cannot manufacture.

For many Filipinos, this psalm touches a tender place. We are a people who know kayod, the grinding work that keeps a family afloat. We know the mother abroad who works a double shift so that tuition gets paid back home, the call center agent who sleeps while the sun is up, the father who lies awake at two in the morning doing the math on rent and rice. Rest can begin to feel like a luxury we cannot afford, or even a small betrayal of the people depending on us. Psalm 127 speaks gently into that worry. It honors the work, and then it reminds the worker that the house was never held up by their wakefulness alone.

The God who builds the house also keeps the night watch, and he gives to his beloved even while they sleep. Elsewhere David prayed, "In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you alone, LORD, make me dwell in safety" (Psalm 4:8). The safety came from God, which is exactly why the sleep could come in peace. When you finally put your head on the pillow, you are trusting that someone else is awake.

Tonight, before you sleep, you might try a small practice. Name the one thing you could not finish today, the unpaid bill or the unresolved argument or the worry about a child, and say it aloud to God as you would hand a bag to a trusted friend at the door. Then pray David's line from Psalm 4:8 and let your body do what it was made to do. If you work nights and your rest comes at noon with the curtains drawn, it is every bit as much a gift, given by the same faithful hands.

Somewhere in the quiet, while you are unaware, your body will be clearing away the debris of the day, the way it has every night of your life. You did not invent that mercy, and you do not have to earn it. You are loved by the Lord, and he has always done some of his finest work while his beloved were fast asleep.

articles.title: The Letter Pepsi Sent Back
articles.dek: In 2006, Coca-Cola's fiercest rival was handed its secrets and mailed them home instead. An old proverb about feeding your enemy shows why that kind of decency carries so much power.
articles.quote: Every time you set food before someone who has hurt you, you are telling a small version of the story of how God won you.
articles.body:
In May 2006, an envelope arrived at PepsiCo headquarters in Purchase, New York. It was a Coca-Cola envelope, and the letter inside came from someone who called himself "Dirk." He said he worked at a high level inside Coca-Cola and could supply confidential material, including details of a product the company had not yet launched. For the right price, the crown jewels of the world's most famous beverage rivalry could belong to Pepsi. For decades the two companies had fought over every shelf, every stadium, and every sari-sari store cooler from Atlanta to Aparri, and here was a shortcut to winning that most executives would only dream about.

Pepsi did something few expected. Within days, its people forwarded the letter to Coca-Cola. Coca-Cola called the FBI, and an undercover agent, posing as a Pepsi executive, met the sellers. Investigators found that an administrative assistant in Coke's own offices had been taking documents and a product sample out of the building. She and two accomplices were arrested that July and later convicted. When reporters asked Pepsi why it had protected its archrival, a spokesman gave a calm answer: "We only did what any responsible company would do. Competition can sometimes be fierce, but also must be fair and legal." Coca-Cola publicly thanked its competitor. In a business famous for its knives, one company had handed the other a cup of water.

Three thousand years earlier, a proverb had described that very moment. Proverbs 25 opens with a note that these sayings of Solomon were "compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah" (Proverbs 25:1). Hezekiah's scribes were gathering wisdom for a nation that lived among hostile neighbors, in towns where feuds between clans could run for generations. Just before this collection, the book had already warned, "Do not gloat when your enemy falls" (Proverbs 24:17), and "Do not say, 'I'll do to them as they have done to me'" (Proverbs 24:29). Then, tucked between a saying about weather and a wry line about a quarrelsome household, comes one of the boldest instructions in the whole book.

"If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat; if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. In doing this, you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you." (Proverbs 25:21–22)

The Hebrew word for "enemy" here is sone'aka, which literally means "the one who hates you." Solomon is describing a real adversary, the person who has wished you harm and perhaps worked toward it, rather than a stranger or a mild annoyance. And the moment he pictures is the moment of that person's weakness. He is hungry. He is thirsty. In the dry hills of Judah, where water came from cisterns and wells that families guarded carefully, controlling someone's access to water was a kind of power. The proverb places that power in your hands and asks you to use it to keep your enemy alive.

Then comes the strange phrase about "burning coals." Readers have puzzled over it for centuries, and it helps to know that the image is about a change of heart rather than a hidden way to hurt someone. Some scholars point to an ancient Egyptian text describing a person who showed repentance by carrying a dish of burning coals on his head, a public sign of a burning conscience. Whether or not that background is behind Solomon's words, the meaning across Scripture is consistent: unexpected kindness produces a fierce, inward heat in the one who receives it. Shame and wonder rise together. The enemy expected a blow and received bread, and that contradiction burns its way into his thinking. Your kindness becomes the most uncomfortable and the most hopeful thing that has happened to him in a long time.

The last phrase is just as rich. "The LORD will reward you" translates the Hebrew yeshallem lak. The verb comes from the root shalam, the same family of words that gives us shalom, God's deep peace and wholeness. To "reward" in this sense is to repay, to make complete, to settle the account fully. One way to read the promise is this: when you refuse to settle the score yourself, God takes the ledger into his own hands, and he settles it in the direction of peace. You let go of being repaid by your enemy, and the Lord himself becomes the one who makes you whole.

The apostle Paul loved this proverb enough to quote it almost word for word. Writing to Christians in Rome who lived under suspicion and sometimes open hostility, he said, "On the contrary: 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. In doing this, you will heap burning coals on his head.' Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (Romans 12:20–21). For Paul, Solomon's practical advice had become something larger, because he had seen it lived out by God himself. Earlier in the same letter, he wrote, "For if, while we were God's enemies, we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through his life!" (Romans 5:10).

This is where the proverb opens into the gospel, the good news about Jesus. We were the hungry enemy. We had turned our backs on God, and he had every right to let us go thirsty. Instead, he set a table. Jesus fed the crowds who would later call for his death, washed the feet of the friend who would deny him, and offered his own body and blood as bread and wine to people who did not deserve a crumb. The burning coals of that kindness are what melt a hard heart. Most of us were never argued into faith. We were undone by a love that came to us while we were still opponents. Every time you set food before someone who has hurt you, you are telling a small version of the story of how God won you.

For most of us, the enemy is closer than a rival corporation. It may be the officemate who took credit for your project, the relative who said cruel things at the last family gathering, the neighbor whose dispute with you has lasted longer than anyone can remember, or the former friend whose name still tightens your chest. Proverbs does not ask you to pretend the hurt never happened or to place yourself back within reach of someone dangerous. Wisdom still sets boundaries. The proverb asks something more specific and more practical: when that person is in need and you have the means to help, you help.

The Pepsi story shows how ordinary this can look. Nobody at Pepsi gave a speech about loving its competitor. Someone simply saw a chance to take advantage of a rival's weakness and chose integrity instead, with a phone call and a forwarded letter. Your version may be equally plain. You might cover a shift for the coworker who undermined you when her child gets sick, send a meal to the in-law who has been cold to you when he is hospitalized, or speak well of a rival in a meeting when it would be easy to stay silent. Each of these is a cup of water placed in an enemy's hand, and each one leaves the outcome with God.

That last part is where freedom lives. You cannot control whether your enemy repents, whether the coals do their work, or whether the relationship is ever repaired. Those things belong to the Lord. What belongs to you is the next kind act, and the promise that the God of shalom sees it and will make you whole. So think today of one person who has made your life harder, and ask the Lord to show you one small need of theirs you could quietly meet this week. Then meet it, and trust him with the rest, remembering the table he once spread for you.
